group.title: Opinion and argument
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To say that something is true, often without proof.
examples: She {claims} that the story is false.
wrong: I claim a thing when I do not say anything about it.

words.meaning: To state something firmly.
examples: He {asserted} that he had done nothing wrong.
wrong: We assert a fact when we are not sure and whisper it quietly.

words.meaning: To feel unsure about something.
examples: I {doubt} that he will come.
wrong: I doubt something when I am completely sure it is true.

words.meaning: To make someone believe something.
examples: I tried to {convince} him to join us.
wrong: I convince a person when I force them not to believe anything.

words.meaning: To make someone do something by giving reasons.
examples: She {persuaded} me to apply for the job.
wrong: I persuade a person when I never give any reason.

words.meaning: To have a different opinion.
examples: I {disagree} with your idea.
wrong: I disagree when I think exactly the same as you.

words.meaning: To say what you think is wrong with someone or something.
examples: People {criticize} the plan for being too expensive.
wrong: We criticize a plan when we praise it warmly.

words.meaning: To agree with and help an idea or a person.
examples: Most people {support} the new law.
wrong: People support a plan when they work against it.

words.meaning: To disagree strongly with something and try to stop it.
examples: Many residents {oppose} the new road.
wrong: We oppose a plan when we are happy to help it.

words.meaning: Causing a lot of disagreement.
examples: The decision was very {controversial}.
wrong: The decision was controversial because everyone agreed at once.

words.meaning: Fair and sensible.
examples: That is a {reasonable} price.
wrong: The price is reasonable because it is too high for anyone.

words.meaning: Based on clear thinking.
examples: It is {logical} to check the facts first.
wrong: It is logical to decide without any thinking.

words.meaning: Unfairly favoring one side.
examples: The judge was {biased} against the team.
wrong: A biased judge treats everyone exactly the same way.

words.meaning: Based on personal feelings rather than facts.
examples: Taste in music is {subjective}.
wrong: A subjective opinion is a fact that anyone can measure.

words.meaning: To make something seem bigger or better than it is.
examples: Don’t {exaggerate}; it was not that bad.
wrong: We exaggerate when we make things seem smaller and tell the exact truth.

words.meaning: To agree that something is true, often unwillingly.
examples: He had to {admit} that he was wrong.
wrong: We admit a mistake when we say we did nothing wrong.

words.meaning: To say that something is not true.
examples: She {denied} taking the money.
wrong: We deny something when we say that it is true and we agree.

words.meaning: To say firmly that something must happen.
examples: I {insist} on paying for dinner.
wrong: I insist when I do not mind and let others decide.

words.meaning: To offer an idea for someone to consider.
examples: I {suggest} that we take a break.
wrong: I suggest an idea when I give an order and nobody can choose.

words.meaning: To say that something is good and should be chosen.
examples: I {recommend} the fish here.
wrong: I recommend a restaurant when I say that nobody should go there.

words.meaning: To say what you think will happen.
examples: Experts {predict} that prices will rise.
wrong: We predict an event after it has already happened.

words.meaning: To suggest something without saying it directly.
examples: Her smile seemed to {imply} that she agreed.
wrong: I imply something when I say it directly in plain words.

words.meaning: To show that something is right or reasonable.
examples: How can you {justify} such a high price?
wrong: We justify a decision when we cannot give any reason.

words.meaning: Facts that show something is true.
examples: Do you have any {proof} of your claim?
wrong: Proof is a guess that nobody can check.

words.meaning: Reasonable, or allowed by the rules.
examples: That is a {valid} point.
wrong: A valid ticket is a ticket that is not good any more.

words.meaning: A fault or a lack of strength.
examples: Lack of time is the main {weakness} of this plan.
wrong: A weakness is the best part of a plan.

words.meaning: Something that helps you do better than others.
examples: Speaking two languages is a big {advantage}.
wrong: An advantage is a problem that makes your job harder.

words.meaning: Something that makes things more difficult.
examples: The main {disadvantage} of the flat is the noise.
wrong: A disadvantage is a benefit that helps you win.

words.meaning: A discussion in which people give different opinions.
examples: There was a long {debate} about the new road.
wrong: A debate is a meeting where nobody speaks.

words.meaning: General agreement among a group.
examples: The team reached a {consensus} after a long talk.
wrong: A consensus is a fight in which nobody agrees on anything.

words.meaning: An agreement in which each side gives up something.
examples: We found a {compromise} on the price.
wrong: A compromise is a decision in which one side wins everything.

words.meaning: A particular way of thinking about something.
examples: Try to see the problem from her {perspective}.
wrong: A perspective is a type of machine for cutting wood.

words.meaning: A person’s way of seeing or judging something.
examples: From my {viewpoint}, the plan is too risky.
wrong: A viewpoint is a fact that is true for everyone.

words.meaning: The way you think or feel about something.
examples: She has a positive {attitude} to work.
wrong: An attitude is the height of a mountain.

words.meaning: A public position on an issue.
examples: The party took a firm {stance} on taxes.
wrong: A stance is a type of food.

words.meaning: Not willing and slow to do something.
examples: He was {reluctant} to speak in public.
wrong: She was reluctant because she was eager and ran to do it.

words.meaning: Doubting that something is true or good.
examples: I am {skeptical} about his promise.
wrong: I am skeptical because I believe everything he says.

words.meaning: Completely sure about something.
examples: I am {convinced} that she is right.
wrong: I am convinced, so I have no idea and I am not sure at all.

words.meaning: Not yet having made a choice.
examples: I am still {undecided} about the job.
wrong: I am undecided, so I made my final choice an hour ago.

words.meaning: Good at making people believe or do something.
examples: She gave a very {persuasive} speech.
wrong: A persuasive speech makes nobody change their mind.
